recentItems.title: The struggles with mental health and suicide prevention in the NT | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
A warning this story contains content some viewers might find distressing.

The Northern Territory is in the midst of a mental health crisis – as it has been for decades. 

Reporter Tilda Colling has been investigating where the gaps are, and whats needed to fix it.

She sat down with three people who struggle with mental illness in the NT, and now use their experience to help as peer support workers.

If this story has raised any concerns for you or someone you know, please contact Lifeline on 13 11 14, or the Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467.

recentItems.title: AI will be deflationary in the long-term, says US investment giant | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
President of US investment giant Northern Trust Asset Management, Michael Hunstad says AI may be the biggest positive supply shock that the global economy has ever seen. 

He says those adopting AI now are already starting to see some pockets of productivity gains - albeit hit and miss, but US technology firms are seeing most of the gains because they were the earlier adopters of AI. Dr Hunstad says they're the first beneficiaries of AI.

He says he believes in the long-term, AI is going to be deflationary.

When asked, however, whether the cost of establishing data centres and buying into AI technology will make the fight against inflation and interest rate settings more difficult for business, he said: "I think over the short term that may be true, but over the longer term, I'm a firm believer that AI may be the biggest positive supply shock that the global economy has ever seen. Ultimately, that's going to be deflationary in the context that is going to bring unit price costs down."

Northern Trust Asset Management has $US1.8 trillion under management.

recentItems.title: Bathla shaping up to be largest housing collapse Australia has ever seen, says property developer
recentItems.description:
The Bathla collapse is a disaster for buyers, subcontractors and lenders, but there are claims it's also set to become the biggest housing collapse in Australian history.

Industry insiders say the fallout could top $4 billion.

Michael Akkawi, the founder and chief executive of prominent developer, Conquest,  a company with major housing projects in Sydney, Airlie Beach and London, says his assessment is that Bathla is shaping up to be the largest corporate collapse Australia has ever seen is because of the size and scale.

"It would be second only to the HIH collapse (in 2001)...This is actually larger than the Babcock collapse back in 2009," he says.

"Based on the numbers that they're reporting at the moment, it's circa $3.6 billion in debt, when you add the layers of subcontractors, suppliers, tax debt, and everyone else in the food chain, that number could be astronomically higher."

Angry sub-contractors are losing hope as a final shutdown looms, and some have been seen going into construction sites to take back materials and appliances in an effort to recoup costs.

Ultimately, Mr Akkawi says Bathla will go into liquidation, describing it as a 'disaster' for people waiting on securing keys to their homes.

Mr Akkawi says the wider problems of high construction costs, government tax changes and interest rate hikes are a 'wake-up call' for the industry.

recentItems.title: House prices plunge as property downturn spreads | The Business | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
House prices have declined for the fifth month in a row, suggesting the property slump won't be stopping any time soon.  The national property market has been hit by several headwinds in recent months, including three Reserve Bank interest rate hikes, and the federal government's decision to restrict negative gearing and increase capital gains tax. Ray White chief economist Nerida Conisbee said fewer properties were coming to market, while Cotality's Gerard Burg said there's lots of doubt about whether or not now is a good time to buy a home.  Housing values are expected to keep falling, particularly if the Reserve Bank lifts interest rates again, which is now seen as more likely to happen.

Meanwhile, one state has announced a crackdown on real estate agent underquoting. From October, sellers in Victoria will be forced to publish the reserve price of their properties at least seven days before it is sold or goes to auction.

recentItems.title: Surgeon performs toe-to-thumb transfer for injured worker on Sunshine Coast | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
When an East Timorese immigrant in Queensland lost her thumb in a workplace accident, she was "very sad" and feared the worst. But eight months later, her surgeon has given her hope.
Dr Chandan Jadhav used Francisca Amaral's second toe to perform the Sunshine Coast's first ever toe-to-thumb transfer.
He said his patient's joy is what "truly defines" his purpose as a plastic surgeon.

recentItems.title: Granville first responders recognised almost 50 years after fatal train crash | ABC NEWS
recentItems.description:
First responders at the Granville rail disaster are being recognised with Australian Bravery Decorations.
 
The 1977 crash killed 85 people and more than 200 others were injured, making it Australia's worst train accident.
 
Other recipients of the award include a retired lawyer who helped stop a man wielding a knife through Sydney's CBD.
